title: Pick the Fastest Path: 6s to 9s
goal: I can pick the fastest shortcut for any 6, 7, 8 or 9 fact and prove my answer.

card.desc: The Prove it lesson for the 6–9 facts. Bailey mixes all four tools (×9 = ×10 − one group, ×6 = ×5 + one group, ×8 = three doubles, ×7 = ×5 + ×2), chooses the shortest path for each fact, previews fact families, and solves mixed word problems. New words: missing factor, operation, versatile, evaluate, demonstrate, inventive, victorious.

win: Victorious! You picked the fastest path every time.

slides.title: Pick the Fastest Path on Your Own
slides.text: In class you proved you can pick the right tool for any 6, 7, 8 or 9 fact. Now do it on your own. You will type most answers. Finish with Show What You Know.

slides.title: Your toolbox
slides.text: Find the hard factor. Pick its tool.
slides.tip: Equal groups? Multiply. Two different amounts put together? Add.

slides.title: Your 7 words
slides.text: Flip each card one more time. Next you will type these words from memory.

words.meaning: the factor you have to find when the product is already given
a math action: add, subtract, multiply, or divide
words.example: Equal groups tell me the operation is multiplication.

words.meaning: able to be used in many different ways
words.example: Doubling is a versatile tool: it works for ×2, ×4 and ×8.

words.meaning: to judge how good something is, or which choice is best
words.example: Hiccup had to evaluate each plan before he picked one.

words.meaning: to show clearly how something works or why it is true
good at thinking of new and clever ideas
words.example: An inventive Viking made a fish trap from a stick and a rope.

words.meaning: having won a fight, a game, or a contest
words.example: The team marched home victorious after the big race.

slides.title: Type the word
slides.text: Type the word that fits. Spell it carefully.

items.q: Which word means a math action: add, subtract, multiply, or divide?
items.no: Look back at the word cards. It starts with o.

items.q: Which word means to judge how good something is, or which choice is best?
items.why: To evaluate is to judge which choice is best.
items.no: It starts with e.

items.q: Use one of your new words. Hiccup used a rope and a bent stick to make a fish trap. He is ____.
items.why: Inventive means good at thinking of new and clever ideas.
items.no: Which word means good at new ideas?

items.q: In 8 × ? = 48, the number you must find is called the ____ ____. (two words)
items.why: The missing factor is the factor you find when the product is given. Here it is 6.
items.no: Two words. The second word is factor.

slides.title: Pick a tool, type the product
slides.text: Use the fastest tool. No adding over and over!

items.no: Use ×10 take away one group.
Use the 6: five 7s plus one more 7.
×4 is double, double.

slides.title: Factors and families
slides.text: Type the missing number. Then verify it.

items.no: 9 times what is 72?
What times 7 is 42?
The family uses only 6, 9 and 54. Which one is missing?

slides.title: Add or multiply?
slides.text: Tap a story, then tap the right box. Ask: equal groups or not?

items.text: 8 boxes with 6 eggs in each box
items.hint: Does every box have the same number?

items.text: Hiccup has 9 coins. Fishlegs has 7 coins.
items.hint: Are these equal groups, or two amounts?

items.text: 7 weeks, with 7 days in each week
items.hint: Does every week have the same number of days?

items.text: Stoick has 6 shields and finds 8 more

items.hint: Does every dragon have the same number of legs?

items.text: 8 Vikings in one boat and 9 in another boat
items.hint: Do both boats hold the same number?

slides.done: Equal groups → multiply. Different amounts put together → add.

slides.title: Teach someone at home
slides.text: Find someone at home. Teach them for two minutes.
prompts: Show them your four tools. Do one fact with each tool.
Demonstrate the 7, 8, 56 fact family: say all four facts.
Tell them about a time Hiccup was victorious, or inventive.

slides.title: Problems from Berk
slides.text: Equal groups or not? Then pick your tool.

items.q: Stoick sends 8 ships. Each ship carries 9 sheep. How many sheep?
items.no: 8 equal groups of 9.

items.q: Fishlegs has 7 jars with 6 beetles in each jar. Then he finds 9 more beetles. How many beetles now?
items.no: First find the beetles in the jars (7 × 6). Then add 9.

items.q: Which fact is NOT in the 8, 7, 56 fact family?
items.why: A fact family uses only 8, 7 and 56 with × and ÷. 56 − 8 = 48 is subtraction and brings in 48.
no: 7 × 8 = 56 proves it. It is in the family.
It is in the family.
8 × 7 = 56 proves it. It is in the family.

sets.why: Break one 7 into 5 + 2: 35 + 14 = 49.
sets.no: Use the ×7 tool: five 7s plus two 7s.

sets.q: On a Viking ship, a rope is versatile. What does that mean?
choices: It is too heavy to carry.
It can be used for many different jobs.
sets.why: Versatile means able to be used in many different ways: tying, pulling, climbing.
no: Versatile is about many uses, not age.
Versatile is about many uses, not weight.
Versatile is about many uses, not who owns it.

sets.q: Which is the fastest path for 8 × 4?
sets.why: Turn it around: 4 × 8 is only two doubles: 16, 32.
no: That works but takes seven adds.
That is the ×9 tool. It finds 9 × 4.
That is not 8 × 4. The 2 was never multiplied.

sets.q: Which fact is NOT in the 7, 9, 63 fact family?
sets.why: 63 is the product, so it is never a factor. 7 × 63 is much bigger than 9.
no: 9 × 7 = 63 is in the family.
63 ÷ 7 = 9 is in the family.
63 ÷ 9 = 7 is in the family.

sets.q: Hiccup shares 63 fish equally among 7 dragons. Which operation finds each dragon's share? Type add, subtract, multiply or divide.
sets.why: Sharing a total into equal groups is division: 63 ÷ 7 = 9, because 7 × 9 = 63.
sets.no: He is sharing a total into equal groups.

sets.q: Stoick has 6 boxes with 9 arrows in each box, plus 5 loose arrows. How many arrows in all?
sets.no: First find the arrows in the boxes (6 × 9). Then add the 5 loose ones.

sets.q: Which word means to show clearly how something works or why it is true?
sets.why: To demonstrate is to show clearly how something works or why it is true.

sets.q: Snotlout says 7 × 6 = 48. Which is the best way to show he is wrong?
choices: 48 is too big for a 7s fact.
sets.why: A break-apart proves 7 × 6 = 42.
no: 42 is even too. Being even doesn't prove it wrong.
7 × 8 = 56 is a 7s fact bigger than 48. Size doesn't prove it.
Ending in 8 doesn't prove anything. Work out the fact.

sets.no: Use the 9: ×10, take away one group of 7.

sets.q: Which Viking is the most inventive?
choices: Snotlout copies whatever the others do.
Hiccup makes a brand-new kind of fish trap that no one has tried before.
Fishlegs reads the same page again.
sets.why: Inventive means good at thinking of new and clever ideas. A brand-new fish trap is a new idea.
no: Copying is the opposite of a new idea.
Reading again is careful, but it is not a new idea.
Shouting is loud, not inventive.

sets.q: Which is the fastest path for 9 × 3?
sets.why: Use the 9: ten 3s is 30, take away one 3. One step: 27.
no: That works, but nine adds is the slowest road.
Three doubles is the ×8 tool. That finds 8 × 3 = 24.
That is the ×7 tool. It finds 7 × 3 = 21.

sets.q: Which fact is in the 7, 6, 42 fact family?
sets.why: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 uses the same three numbers. 6 × 7 = 42 proves it.
no: Subtraction is not in this fact family, and 36 is not one of the numbers.
Addition is not in this fact family.
42 is the product, so it is never a factor.

sets.q: 8 dragons each eat 9 fish. Which operation finds how many fish they eat in all? Type add, subtract, multiply or divide.
sets.why: Each dragon eats 9: equal groups. Multiply: 8 × 9 = 72.
sets.no: Each dragon eats the same amount. Equal groups or not?

sets.q: Fishlegs has 7 bags with 7 rocks in each bag, plus 6 loose rocks. How many rocks in all?
sets.no: First find the rocks in the bags (7 × 7). Then add 6.

sets.q: Which word means having won a fight, a game, or a contest?
sets.why: Victorious means having won.

sets.q: Fishlegs says 9 × 7 = 56. Which is the best way to show he is wrong?
choices: 9 × 7 is a 9s fact, so it must end in 9.
sets.why: The ×9 tool proves 9 × 7 = 63. (56 is 7 × 8.)
no: Even numbers can be 9s facts too, like 72. That doesn't prove it.
9 × 7 = 63 ends in 3. That rule is false.
56 is too small, not too big. 9 × 7 = 63.

sets.no: Use ×5 plus one group, or three doubles.
What times 9 is 81? Try the ×9 tool.

sets.q: Hiccup must evaluate two plans. What does he do?
choices: He tries both plans at the same time.
He writes the plans in a secret code.
He judges which plan is better.
sets.why: To evaluate is to judge how good something is, or which choice is best.
no: Trying both is not judging them.
Forgetting is not judging.
Writing in code is not judging.

sets.q: Which is the fastest path for 7 × 8?
sets.why: 5, 6, 7, 8: 56 = 7 × 8. One step to remember.
no: That works but takes six adds.
That mixes up the ×9 tool. It is wrong.
That doubles the 8, which finds 8 × 8.

sets.q: Which fact is NOT in the 8, 9, 72 fact family?
sets.why: 72 ÷ 8 = 9, not 8. That fact is false.
no: 9 × 8 = 72 proves it. It is in the family.
It is in the family.
It is in the family.

sets.q: Stoick has 7 shields. Gobber has 9 shields. Which operation finds how many shields they have in all? Type add, subtract, multiply or divide.
sets.why: Two different amounts put together. Not equal groups, so add: 7 + 9 = 16.
sets.no: Are these equal groups, or two different amounts?

sets.q: A Viking trader has 9 racks with 6 axes on each rack. He sells 4 axes. How many axes are left?
sets.no: First find all the axes (9 × 6). Then take away 4.

sets.q: Which word means able to be used in many different ways?
sets.why: Versatile means able to be used in many different ways.

sets.q: In 9 × ? = 63, what is the missing factor?
sets.why: 9 × 7 = 70 − 7 = 63, so the missing factor is 7.
no: 63 is the product, not the missing factor.
9 is the factor you already have.
70 is 7 × 10, the first step of the ×9 tool. Take away one 7 to get 63.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one. Only your first try counts. Type most answers. Pick the fastest tool.

questions.why: Use the 9: four 10s is 40, take away one 4: 40 − 4 = 36.
questions.no: Use the 9: ×10, take away one group of 4.

no: 18 is 6 × 3. You need one more 3.
24 is 8 × 3. One group too many.
10 is 7 + 3. Multiply, do not add.

questions.no: 6 times what is 36? Use ×5 plus one group.

no: That adds 7 each time. Doubling 14 jumps straight to 28.
That is three doubles of 4, which is 8 × 4 = 32.

questions.q: Which fact belongs to the 8, 6, 48 fact family?
questions.why: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 uses the same three numbers. 6 × 8 = 48 proves it.
no: Subtraction is not part of this fact family, and 40 is not one of the numbers.
Addition is not part of a multiplication fact family.

questions.q: Which fact is the commutative partner of 9 × 7?
no: 9 × 9 changes a factor. Commutative only switches the order.
That is in the fact family, but it is division. Switch the factors instead.

choices: carry out both plans at once
questions.why: To evaluate is to judge how good something is.
no: Doing both is not judging them. Evaluate means decide which is better.
Writing plans down is a good start, but evaluating means judging which is better.
Mixing plans is not judging them. Evaluate means decide which is better.

questions.q: Use one of your new words. Hiccup thinks of a brand-new way to cross the river. He is ____.
questions.why: Inventive means good at thinking of new and clever ideas.
questions.no: Which word means good at new ideas? It starts with in.

questions.q: A dragon trainer has 9 dragons. Each dragon eats 6 fish at dinner. How many fish?
questions.no: 9 equal groups of 6. Use ×10 take away one group.

questions.q: Hiccup's team won the race. Hiccup was victorious. What does that mean?
choices: He was worried he would fail.
questions.why: Victorious means having won a fight, a game, or a contest.
no: His team already won, so he is not worried. Victorious means he won.
Victorious is about winning, not about being bored.

teacher.objective: Bailey proves the 6–9 facts: she chooses the fastest of her four tools for any fact, checks answers with a second tool, finds missing factors, sees the four facts in a fact family, and solves mixed word problems (including one that is addition, not multiplication). New words: missing factor, operation, versatile, evaluate, demonstrate, inventive, victorious.
materials: 16 index cards, one 6–9 fact on each (for the tool sort)
About 60 counters for the 7 × 8 fact family array
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Her Lesson 3 packet and Lesson 4 packet page 1 to check
Lesson 5 packet printed to send home
Optional: a phone timer for the quick-fire

plan.do: Class slide 1. Check the Lesson 3 packet and Lesson 4 packet page 1 (praise one thing, fix one thing). She names her four tools.
Class slide 2. She compares two plans from the book and evaluates which was better.
Class slide 3. She says each tool aloud before tapping.
Class slides 4–5. Teach the 7 words one at a time; add the index cards to the pile. She demonstrates 8 × 6 out loud.
Class slides 6–7. She sorts 16 fact cards into 4 tool piles and answers each; then the timed quick-fire, naming each tool.
Class slide 8. She evaluates each path out loud: does it work, how many steps?
Class slides 9–10. 7 rows of 8 counters: turn it for 8 × 7, share 56 into 8 rows for 56 ÷ 8. Preview only.
Class slides 11–12. She says each step aloud and asks "equal groups or not?" before every problem.
Class slide 13. She types the operation, then solves on the whiteboard.
Class slide 14. She picks index cards and defends a tool for each, demonstrating 6 × 9 two ways.
Class slide 15. Go through the task list and the Times Table Trail links. Hand her the Lesson 5 packet. Celebrate two weeks of fact tools.

watch: Going back to adding 7s or 8s over and over when a fact feels hard. Ask: "Which tool is that factor's tool?"
Picking the longest path for two-hard-factor facts (7 × 9 by 45 + 18 when 70 − 7 is faster). Praise that it works, then ask which has fewer steps.
Multiplying in an addition story (9 fish + 8 fish = 72). Have her say "equal groups or not?" before every problem.
Mixing up commutative (switch factors) with the division facts in a fact family. Use the triangle: the top number is the product.
"I can't do it." Hand her the index card and ask for just the tool name first, then just the first step.

packet_key.answer: missing factor: the factor you must find when the product is given
operation: add, subtract, multiply, or divide
versatile: able to be used in many ways
evaluate: to judge which choice is best
demonstrate: to show clearly why something is true
inventive: good at thinking of new, clever ideas
Any sentence using victorious as having won, e.g. "Hiccup was victorious when his plan beat the dragon."
Best: ×9 tool, 70 − 7 = 63, because it is one step. Accept 45 + 18 = 63 with a clear reason.

If she is at 90 or above, Monday goes straight to the area model.

Saturday: do page 2 of the Lesson 4 Packet.

slides.title: Pick the Fastest Path: 6s to 9s
slides.text: In two weeks you collected four tools for the hard facts. Today you prove you can pick the right tool for each fact, fast, and explain why it works.

notes.do: Check her Lesson 3 packet and Lesson 4 packet page 1 before you start: praise one thing, fix one thing. Look at her Lesson 4 after-class score.
notes.say: "Two weeks, four tools. Today you prove you can pick the right tool fast and explain why it works."
notes.ask: "Name your four tools. Which number does each one go with?"
notes.listen: "9: ten groups take one away. 6: five groups add one. 8: double three times. 7: five groups plus two groups."

slides.title: Which plan worked better?
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: What happened in the part you read since Tuesday's lesson?
Think of two different plans or ways characters tried to solve a problem. Which one worked better? Why?
Hiccup does not have big muscles. What does he have instead that helps him most? Give a reason from the book.
starters: Hiccup's best tool is … For example, …

notes.do: 5–7 minutes. Today's reading skill matches today's math skill: evaluate which plan is better.
notes.ask: "Think of two different plans characters tried. Which worked better? Why?" "What does Hiccup have instead of muscles?"
notes.listen: Two real plans compared with a reason ("… worked better because …"). For Hiccup: brains, watching, planning, kindness, with an example.

items.q: What is 7 × 7? Break the 7 into 5 + 2.
no: 42 is 6 × 7. The bottom part is 2 sevens, so add 14, not 7.
56 is 8 × 7. That is one seven too many.

items.q: Bailey knows 8 groups of 6 is 48. She takes half of the groups. Which fact does she get?
items.why: Half of 8 groups is 4 groups of 6: 4 × 6 = 24, which is half of 48.
no: Only the number of groups was halved. Each group still has 6.
Half of 8 groups is 4 groups, not 6. And half of 48 is 24, not 36.

items.q: Which word means to break a number into smaller parts?
items.why: To decompose 7 is to break it into 5 + 2.
no: Reassemble is the opposite: putting the parts back together.
A fragment is a broken piece, but the action word for breaking a number apart is decompose.

notes.do: She says the tool out loud before each tap.
notes.listen: "42 is 6 × 7. The bottom part is 2 sevens, 14, so 35 + 14 = 49."

slides.title: Seven words for today
slides.text: Jonathan teaches each word. Flip the card, read the meaning, and make your own sentence.

words.meaning: the factor you have to find when the product is already given
a math action: add, subtract, multiply, or divide
words.example: Equal groups tell me the operation is multiplication.

words.meaning: able to be used in many different ways
words.example: Doubling is a versatile tool: it works for ×2, ×4 and ×8.

words.meaning: to judge how good something is, or which choice is best
words.example: Hiccup had to evaluate each plan before he picked one.

words.meaning: to show clearly how something works or why it is true
good at thinking of new and clever ideas
words.example: An inventive Viking made a fish trap from a stick and a rope.

words.meaning: having won a fight, a game, or a contest
words.example: The team marched home victorious after the big race.

notes.do: Teach one word at a time (about 1 minute each). Write each word on an index card and add it to her word pile.
notes.say: "A missing factor is the factor you have to find. An operation is a math action: add, subtract, multiply or divide. Versatile means it can do many jobs, like a Swiss army knife. To evaluate is to judge which is best. To demonstrate is to show clearly. Inventive people think of new ideas. Victorious means you won."
notes.ask: "Which of your four tools is the most versatile? Why?" "Demonstrate 8 × 6 for me." "When were you victorious?"
notes.listen: "Doubling, because it works for ×2, ×4 and ×8." "6, 12, 24, 48." A real personal win.

items.q: Hiccup's knife can cut rope, carve wood, and open shells. Which word best describes the knife?
items.why: Versatile means it can be used in many different ways.
no: Victorious describes someone who won. A knife cannot win.
An operation is a math action like add or multiply.
Inventive describes a person who thinks of new ideas. The knife is a tool that can do many jobs.

items.q: Bailey says 7 × 9 = 63. Which answer best demonstrates that it is true?
choices: "63 is a big number, so it fits."
items.why: To demonstrate is to show clearly why it is true. The ×9 tool shows it.
no: Being sure is a feeling, not a reason. Show how you know.
Lots of facts are big numbers. That does not prove 63 is right.

items.q: Hiccup is good at thinking of new and clever ideas. Which word describes him? Type it.
items.why: Inventive means good at thinking of new and clever ideas.
items.no: It starts with in.

notes.do: She answers out loud first and explains each wrong choice.
notes.ask: "Why is the knife versatile but not inventive?"
notes.listen: "A knife can do many jobs, but only a person can think of new ideas."

slides.title: Your toolbox
slides.text: Look at the factors first. Find the hard one (6, 7, 8 or 9). Then pick its tool.

visual.text:
🔟 ×9: ×10, then take away one group.  9 × 4 → 40 − 4 = 36
🖐️ ×6: ×5, then add one group.  6 × 3 → 15 + 3 = 18
✌️ ×8: double, double, double.  8 × 5 → 10, 20, 40
🧩 ×7: ×5 plus ×2.  7 × 3 → 15 + 6 = 21

slides.tip: If a fact has two hard factors, like 7 × 9, pick the tool with the fewest steps. A 9 is usually fastest: just one subtraction.

notes.do: Hands-on: spread 16 index cards, one 6–9 fact on each. She sorts them into 4 piles by tool, then answers each card out loud.
notes.say: "Look at the factors first. Find the hard one. Then pick its tool."
notes.ask: For 7 × 9 and 6 × 8: "Both factors are hard. Which tool is shorter? Why?"
notes.listen: "7 × 9: use the 9, 70 − 7, one step." "6 × 8: three doubles of 6, or 40 + 8." Either is fine with a reason.

slides.title: Tool, then answer
slides.text: Say the tool out loud. Then type the product.

items.no: Use the 9: ten 6s is 60. Now take away one 6.
Break one 7 into 5 + 2: five 7s plus two 7s.
The 8 means three doubles. Start with 4.
Use the 6: five 6s plus one more 6.

notes.do: Time it on your phone for fun: can she do all four in under a minute while naming each tool?
notes.ask: "Which one took you the longest? Which tool would make it faster?"
notes.listen: Tool names before answers. If she goes silent and starts counting, say "Which tool?"

slides.title: Pick the fastest path
slides.text: All of these facts have more than one road. Evaluate each path and pick the best one.

items.q: Which is the best path for 8 × 6?
items.why: Three doubles: 6 → 12 → 24 → 48. Three steps, and you can check each one.
no: That adds to 48, but it takes seven steps. That is where counting goes wrong.
60 − 6 is the ×9 tool. It finds 9 × 6, not 8 × 6.

items.q: 7 × 9 has a 7 and a 9. Which path is fastest?
items.why: Use the 9: seven tens is 70, take away one 7. One step: 63.
no: This works too and gives 63! But it needs two facts and a harder add. 70 − 7 is one step.
Skip counting nine times works, but it is the slowest road and easy to lose your place.

items.q: Which is the best path for 6 × 7?
items.why: Use the 6: five 7s is 35, plus one more 7 is 42.
no: 36 is 6 × 6, not 5 × 7. Start with five 7s: 35.
6 + 7 adds the factors. You need 6 groups of 7.

notes.do: Before she taps, she evaluates each path out loud: Does it work? How many steps?
notes.ask: "Path A for 7 × 9 also gives 63. So why isn't it the best?"
notes.listen: "It works, but it needs two facts and a hard add. 70 − 7 is one step."

slides.title: Fact families
slides.text: Three numbers can make four facts. That group is called a fact family. Division undoes multiplication.

steps.text: 56 ÷ 8 = 7 (56 shared into 8 equal groups gives 7 in each)
56 ÷ 7 = 8 (56 shared into 7 equal groups gives 8 in each)

slides.tip: Every multiplication fact you know is also a division fact you know. In two weeks you will use this a lot.

notes.do: Build 7 rows of 8 counters. Turn the array to show 8 × 7. Then share 56 counters into 8 equal rows to show 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Keep it a preview: division is Week 4.
notes.say: "Three numbers, four facts. Division undoes multiplication."
notes.listen: "8." Point at the triangle: the top number is the product.

items.q: Which fact belongs to the 6, 9, 54 fact family?
items.why: 54 ÷ 9 = 6 uses the same three numbers, and 9 × 6 = 54 proves it.
no: Fact families here are multiplication and division, not addition.
That is true math, but subtraction is not part of this fact family, and 45 is not one of the three numbers.

items.q: 7 × ? = 42. What is the missing factor?
no: 7 × 5 = 35. You need one more 7.
7 × 7 = 49. That is too many.
7 × 8 = 56. That is too many.

items.q: Bailey knows 8 × 9 = 72. What does the commutative property give her for free?
items.why: Commutative means switch the order of the factors: 9 × 8 = 72.
no: That is in the same fact family, but it is division. Commutative means switching the factors.
That adds. The commutative property here switches the factors in a multiplication.

notes.do: She uses the triangle on the slide to check each answer.
notes.listen: "45 isn't one of the three numbers, and the family is × and ÷."

slides.title: Solve like a pro
slides.text: Stoick sends 6 ships. Each ship carries 9 sheep. How many sheep? Tap the steps in order.
steps: Read it and find the equal groups: 6 ships, 9 sheep each
Pick the tool: it has a 9, so ×10 and take away one group
Check with another tool, then label: 45 + 9 = 54 ✔, so 54 sheep
slides.why: Read, write the fact, pick the tool, solve, check, label. Two tools gave the same answer, so you know it is right.
slides.hint: What do you do before you can write a fact? You have to read and find the groups.

notes.do: She taps each step and says it out loud.
notes.listen: "If two tools give the same answer, I know it's right."

items.q: Fishlegs collects 6 dragon scales a day for 7 days. How many scales?
no: 13 is 6 + 7. He collects 6 each day, so these are equal groups.
48 is 6 × 8. There are 7 days.
36 is 6 × 6. Count the days again: 7.

items.q: Toothless ate 8 crabs. A gargantuan sea dragon ate 7 times as many. How many crabs did the sea dragon eat?
no: 15 is 8 + 7. "Times as many" means multiply.
64 is 8 × 8. The dragon ate 7 times as many.
49 is 7 × 7. Toothless ate 8 crabs, not 7.

items.q: Hiccup has 9 fish. Fishlegs has 8 fish. How many fish do they have in all?
items.why: These are not equal groups. It is two amounts put together, so add: 9 + 8 = 17.
no: 72 is 9 × 8. Nobody has 9 groups of 8. Read again: two boys, two amounts.
1 is 9 − 8. That tells how many more Hiccup has, not how many in all.
81 is 9 × 9. There are no equal groups here.

notes.do: She reads each problem aloud and says "equal groups or not?" before she taps.
notes.ask: On the 9 + 8 fish problem: "Are there equal groups?"
notes.listen: "No, it's two different amounts put together, so add."

slides.title: Add or multiply?
slides.text: Ask: equal groups or not? Then type the operation.

items.q: The Berk blacksmith has 6 racks with 9 helmets on each rack. Which operation finds how many helmets? Type add, subtract, multiply or divide.
items.why: 6 racks with 9 on EACH rack are equal groups, so multiply: 6 × 9 = 54.
items.no: Each rack has the same number. Equal groups or not?

items.q: Toothless caught 7 fish in the morning and 8 fish at night. Which operation finds how many fish in all? Type add, subtract, multiply or divide.
items.why: Two different amounts put together. Not equal groups, so add: 7 + 8 = 15.
items.no: Is it equal groups, or two amounts put together?

items.q: A gargantuan dragon ate 9 times as many crabs as Toothless. Toothless ate 6. Which operation finds the gargantuan dragon's crabs? Type add, subtract, multiply or divide.
items.no: What does "times as many" tell you?

notes.do: She says "equal groups or not?" out loud for every story, then types the operation, then solves it on the whiteboard.
notes.ask: "What words in the story told you?"
notes.listen: "each" or "times as many" for multiply; "and" or "in all" with two different amounts for add.

slides.title: Defend your tool
slides.text: Jonathan picks a fact. You pick a tool and defend it.
prompts: For 8 × 7, which tool would you use? Evaluate two paths and pick one.
Which of your four tools is the most versatile? Justify your answer.
starters: One way is … Another way is …
The most versatile tool is … because …

notes.do: Use three index cards from the sort pile. She holds up the card and argues for her tool.
notes.say: "There can be more than one good path. I want your reason."
notes.listen: Any correct path with a reason about the number of steps. "60 − 6" and "45 + 9" for 6 × 9.

slides.text: In two weeks you collected four tools, learned to pick the fastest one, and met fact families.
